questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the divergence between a principal's interests and an agent's payment rule
questions.stem: While drafting a brief for a town drainage contract, the engineer notices the firm is paid per load hauled while residents dislike noisy night collections.

options.text: The haulier is the agent and residents are principals whose interests diverge from the payment rule
The town council is the principal and the haulier is the agent, so the two interests are aligned by law
options.misconception: assumes principal and agent interests always coincide

options.text: The engineer is the principal because the brief defines what must be delivered on each collection round
options.misconception: treats the brief author as principal by default

options.text: Both council and haulier are agents of the national works ministry, so the contract has no principal
options.misconception: assumes the state can never be the principal

questions.explanation: Payment by load rewards the haulier for more collections than residents want. Residents bear the noise, so they are the principals whose preferences the agent does not share.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the cost that the payment rule creates.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the principal from who bears the residual cost in a delegated arrangement
questions.stem: A brief annex lists who pays and who benefits from a proposed toll gate: hauliers pay 12 per crossing, the highway authority keeps 70 per cent of that, and residents on the bypass route lose 40 minutes a day.

options.text: The highway authority is the principal because it collects most of the toll revenue each day
options.misconception: assumes whoever collects the money is the principal

options.text: The residents are principals because they bear the time cost while the toll is collected from others
The hauliers are principals because they pay the toll on every single crossing
options.misconception: confuses who pays a fee with who is served

options.text: The brief author is the principal because the annex defines the scheme's purpose
options.misconception: treats the analyst as the principal by default

questions.explanation: The principal is the party whose welfare the delegated activity serves and who bears its residual costs. Residents lose 40 minutes daily but share no revenue, so their interests are what is at stake.
questions.hint: Look for who bears a cost and gains nothing from it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an agency shifts effort away from its original mandate
questions.stem: An engineer's brief for a water authority notes that a reforestation unit originally tasked with planting woodland has spent 90 per cent of its budget on issuing permits to contractors.

options.text: The unit drifted because engineers in the field preferred building work to planting
options.misconception: blames personal preference rather than new incentives

options.text: The unit drifted because the reforestation target was never written into its founding charter
options.misconception: believes a missing charter clause causes drift

options.text: The unit drifted because new permit work carried promotion and budget advantages the planting target lacked
The unit drifted because engineers designed planting targets that were too ambitious for the terrain
options.misconception: explains drift by terrain rather than incentive

questions.explanation: Drift happens when the agent's surroundings reward a different activity from its original mandate. Promotion and budget now follow permit work, so effort tracks those rewards, not the planting target.
questions.hint: Ask what the unit now gains by changing its activity.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a composite corruption index from equally weighted component scores
questions.stem: A corruption exposure index for the engineer's procurement district averages four equally weighted sub-scores of 40, 35, 30 and 31. What is the composite index value?
questions.explanation: The four component scores sum to 136, and equal weighting gives 136 divided by 4, which is 34. Such an index bundles perception signals into one figure rather than counting actual bribe events.
questions.hint: Average the four equally weighted component scores.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh perception and experience measures when choosing a corruption monitoring approach
questions.stem: Asked to recommend how corruption in the district should be monitored, the engineer weighs an expert perception score against the bribery reports collected by clinic staff.

options.text: Use the perception score because it is produced by a consistent panel of analysts each year
options.misconception: assumes consistency proves accuracy of perception scores

options.text: Use staff reports because they cover every clinic and every patient contact in the district
options.misconception: assumes complete coverage of experience surveys

options.text: Use both measures and average them so that no single source can dominate the report
options.misconception: believes averaging cancels out different biases

options.text: Use both measures and report them separately, since perception and experience capture different things

questions.explanation: Perception scores capture what observers believe about a sector; experience measures capture what users report meeting. Averaging hides the gap between them, so the brief should present each series and the gap.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify corruption by scale and reach using a case description

stimulus.body: Our members report two separate problems. A handful of very large tenders appear to be steered toward connected firms, while ordinary permit and inspection visits are settled with small cash payments made to individual staff. The first kind involves a handful of cases; the second touches almost every business we surveyed.

questions.stem: The engineer's brief quotes a local chamber note before awarding the drainage works; the note is reproduced below.

options.text: The note describes both grand and petty corruption as separate problems of scale and reach
The note treats the small payments as grand corruption because each one breaches a legal rule
options.misconception: judges corruption by illegality rather than scale

options.text: The note treats the steered tenders as petty corruption because each affects a single small firm
options.misconception: confuses number of parties with scale of the sum

options.text: The note suggests both kinds are petty because they involve a limited number of transactions
options.misconception: reads a small count of cases as small corruption

questions.explanation: Grand corruption concerns large sums and capture of decisions; petty corruption concerns small, repeated payments to individual staff. The note names one of each, so its scale-based split applies the distinction directly.
questions.hint: Ask what separates the two kinds mentioned in the note.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the systemic and sporadic distinction changes the remedy chosen
questions.stem: A regulator asks the engineer to explain, in a short note for a design brief, why it matters that corruption in the water sector is systemic rather than sporadic.

answer.exemplar: Systemic corruption is embedded in rules and routine practice, so it produces predictable costs for every user and will not be removed by punishing a few individuals. Sporadic corruption is scattered and individual, so a handful of prosecutions can shrink it. Explaining the difference tells the regulator that a sanctions-only response will fail against embedded practice and that procurement and staffing rules must change.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate links the distinction between embedded and scattered corruption to the choice of remedy rather than reciting definitions. A strong answer states why each pattern calls for a different response.
questions.hint: Focus on what each pattern implies for the remedy.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise state capture in a regulator that writes the criteria it applies
questions.stem: A procurement specialist on the engineer's brief observes that the panel which writes tender criteria also receives consultancy fees from the firms it scores.

options.text: The panel has a conflict of interest that a disclosure form and recusal rule would fully remove
options.misconception: believes disclosure alone eliminates the incentive

options.text: The panel's role has been captured, since the firms it scores now shape the criteria it applies
The panel is simply corrupt and must be replaced by an equally external set of assessors
options.misconception: assumes rotation of insiders removes capture

options.text: The panel is only conflicted if a particular tender is later found to be unfairly scored
options.misconception: waits for proven malpractice before naming capture

questions.explanation: Capture occurs when the parties being regulated shape the decisions made about them. Here the scored firms set the criteria and earn fees from the panel, so independence is gone.
questions.hint: Ask who influences the rules the panel applies.

questions.learningObjective: Compare agent payment rules for their alignment with the principal's objective
questions.stem: A brief table shows payment per site for four contractors: one earns 900 per completed household connection, one a flat 800 per street, one 950 per household plus 200 per missed deadline, and one 900 per hour worked.

options.text: The flat street fee creates the weakest incentive to complete every household connection on time
options.misconception: ignores how flat fees interact with workload size

options.text: The 200 per missed deadline is the strongest penalty for lateness because it is paid on delay
options.misconception: misreads a bonus for lateness as a penalty

options.text: Payment per completed connection gives the clearest incentive to finish each connection
The hourly rate gives the clearest incentive to complete connections since hourly pay rewards speed
options.misconception: assumes hourly pay rewards unit completion

questions.explanation: Payment per completed connection ties revenue to the task the principal wants done. A flat street fee rewards effort, hourly pay rewards time, and a bonus for missed deadlines rewards delay.
questions.hint: Ask which pay rule rises with the task's completion.

options.misconception: equates budget control with the principal role

options.text: The residents are principals because they live closest to the works and are most affected
options.misconception: equates proximity with the principal role

options.text: The engineer is the principal because the engineer signs the brief and certifies the design
options.misconception: treats the certifier as the principal

options.text: The principal is whoever's objectives the delegated design serves, here the ministry's timetable

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Quantify the percentage drift between an agency's target and its achievement
questions.stem: A water authority set out in the brief to conserve 80 million litres a day; ten years on it reports conserving 68 million litres a day. By what percentage has it fallen short of its target?

questions.learningObjective: State what a corruption index aggregates and what it cannot be read to mean
questions.stem: The engineer must write a paragraph for the brief explaining why a published corruption index should not be quoted as a count of bribes in the district.

options.text: The index bundles expert or perception signals about how corrupt a sector looks, not a count of bribery cases
The index is drawn from police statistics and so should match the number of prosecutions exactly
options.misconception: assumes every index counts reported cases

options.text: The index is built from surveys of firms and so measures exactly how many firms were asked for money
options.misconception: confuses an experience survey with a bribe count

options.text: The index covers only the largest cities, so district figures cannot be compared with it at all
options.misconception: assumes only geography stops comparison

questions.explanation: An index is a composite judgement about how corrupt a sector appears, usually from expert or public perception. It aids comparison over time but cannot be read as a tally of bribes paid in a district.
questions.hint: Ask what the index actually counts or judges.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a divergence between perception and experience corruption measures

stimulus.body: We hold two series for the district. The first is the annual perception score produced by a panel of outside analysts, which has moved only from 42 to 39 in four years. The second counts what clinic staff say they were asked to pay for certificates during the same period, which fell from 300 cases to 190 cases. The panel number barely shifts while reported experience falls by more than a third.

questions.stem: The engineer's brief cites a comparison of two corruption measures for the same district; the extract is set out below.

options.text: The two series agree, so either measure would give the same account of change in the district
options.misconception: treats both movements as confirming each other

options.text: The gap between the two series means the panel is too slow to register changes that users feel
The fall in reported cases proves that corruption in the district has been eliminated altogether
options.misconception: reads one falling series as total elimination

options.text: The experience series is useless because patients may exaggerate the amounts they are charged
options.misconception: dismisses reported experience without comparing series

questions.explanation: A perception panel can move slowly, tracking overall impressions rather than specific transactions, while reported experience shifts fast when practice changes. Their divergence is itself the finding.
questions.hint: Ask why the two series move by different amounts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish grand from petty corruption and the enforcement each requires
questions.stem: A mayor asks the engineer to explain, for a public design brief, how petty corruption differs from grand corruption and why the difference matters for enforcement.

answer.exemplar: Petty corruption is small-scale, frequent and transactional: a small payment made by an ordinary citizen to obtain a routine service or to speed a routine permit. Grand corruption is large-scale and systematic: tenders steered to connected firms, contracts inflated, licences sold. The difference matters because petty corruption is usually visible, dispersed and removable through rules on payment and supervision, while grand corruption alters the decisions themselves and requires changes to procurement and oversight.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate can state both kinds in behavioural terms and then derive different enforcement consequences from each. A good answer links scale and frequency to the type of remedy, not just to labels.
questions.hint: Tie each kind of corruption to its enforcement route.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an embedded rule at one stage from scattered opportunistic payment
questions.stem: A consultant's note for the engineer's brief warns that the same bribery practice appears in every district of the region, always at the inspection stage.

options.text: The practice is sporadic because it happens in separate districts rather than in one place
options.misconception: reads many locations as many isolated events

options.text: The practice is sporadic because each inspector accepts only a single bribe per year
options.misconception: judges frequency by count per person only

options.text: The practice is systemic because it is a repeated rule embedded in how the inspection stage works
The practice is systemic only if the inspector is unaware that payment is expected of them
options.misconception: requires ignorance for a pattern to be systemic

questions.explanation: Systemic corruption is a standing practice built into how a stage of administration works, recurring in every case handled there. Sporadic corruption is scattered and opportunistic, with no linking rule.
questions.hint: Ask whether the practice follows a rule at one stage.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a capture pattern in the concentration of approvals among thinly established firms
questions.stem: A brief table shows licence applications received and approved by a licensing board over a year: 420 received, 380 approved, and 260 of the approvals to firms that had been trading for only three months.

options.text: The board approves most applications, so it is not captured by any interest group
options.misconception: equates high approval rates with impartiality

options.text: The board is captured because more firms applied than were approved
options.misconception: reads demand for licences as evidence of capture

options.text: The board is captured because sixty per cent of its members own licensed firms
options.misconception: asserts ownership facts the table does not contain

options.text: The pattern fits capture, since approvals concentrate on firms with a thin and recent presence

questions.explanation: Capture shows as decisions bending toward a connected party rather than following published criteria. Concentrated approvals among thinly established firms are consistent with that bending, though not proof.
questions.hint: Ask what distinguishes the firms that win approval.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a fixed payment leaves room for the agent to economise on effort
questions.stem: In the engineer's brief the agent is a construction firm paid a fixed sum, and the principal is the public body that wants the bridge finished on time and within budget.

options.text: A problem arises because the fixed payment lets the firm cut effort while the body needs quality delivered
No problem arises because the fixed sum already removes any incentive to skimp on workmanship
options.misconception: believes fixed payment removes quality incentives

options.text: The problem is only that the public body cannot inspect the bridge after handover
options.misconception: confuses monitoring gaps with incentive conflicts

options.text: No problem arises because a signed contract settles both parties' rights in advance
options.misconception: believes a contract erases divergent interests

questions.explanation: The principal wants quality and timeliness; the agent on a fixed sum keeps more by economising on effort. Where effort is hard to observe, their interests pull apart, which is what the brief must design around.
questions.hint: Ask how a fixed sum could reward lower effort.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the amount tenants lose to the landlord agent above running costs
questions.stem: Tenants in the engineer's surveyed block pay 1,200 a month in rent, of which 300 sits with the landlord agent beyond the cost of running the building. For the block's 240 tenants, what is the annual amount paid to the agent above running costs?
questions.explanation: The portion going to the agent beyond running costs is 300 a month per tenant. For 240 tenants that is 72,000 a month, and over twelve months it reaches 864,000, what the principals lose.
questions.hint: Multiply the monthly excess by tenants and months.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recommend how to prevent agency drift through incentive alignment
questions.stem: The engineer is asked to recommend how to stop a maintenance agency drifting from the brief it was given.

options.text: Write a longer brief, since agencies that receive detailed instructions drift less than those that do not
options.misconception: believes instructions alone prevent drift

options.text: Align promotion, budget and reporting with the original mandate so the agent's rewards follow the brief
Rotate the agency's leadership every three years so that no one can settle into a pattern
options.misconception: presumes leadership rotation corrects incentive drift

options.text: Ask the agency's staff to sign an annual pledge affirming the brief, and publish who signs
options.misconception: confuses pledges with changed incentives

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a case as grand or petty corruption using value and decision level

stimulus.body: Two accounts were sent to us this month. The first concerns a single regional tender for road surfacing where the winning price was well above the published estimate and the bidder shares a director with two firms on the assessment panel. The second concerns routine water connection visits, where our members describe leaving small cash sums with the clerk who signs the permit.

questions.stem: The engineer attaches an extract from a local business group to the brief before recommending a site inspection; the extract reads as follows.

options.text: The two accounts show petty corruption only, because each involves one small firm and one local office
options.misconception: treats local scale as the test for petty corruption

options.text: The two accounts show grand corruption only, because both involve deliberate distortion of a transaction
options.misconception: collapses the scale distinction into intent alone

options.text: The first account is grand and the second is petty, because scale and reach differ sharply between them
The two accounts show sporadic corruption only, because neither describes a practice followed by every official
options.misconception: reads sporadic as if it meant small

questions.explanation: Grand corruption turns on large value and influence over high-level decisions such as a major tender. Petty corruption turns on small routine payments to staff; neither case needs to be everywhere to belong to its category.
questions.hint: Compare the value and the level of each case.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the control frequency differs between embedded and scattered corruption
questions.stem: An oversight officer asks the engineer to explain, in a short paragraph for the brief, why a distinction between systemic and sporadic corruption changes how often a control should be checked.

answer.exemplar: Systemic corruption is built into a routine stage of administration, so it operates on every case that passes through that stage and will reappear unless the rule itself is changed. Sporadic corruption is scattered and opportunistic, so controls can rely on catching individual instances. That is why systemic risk calls for a standing control on every transaction, while sporadic risk calls for spot checks and reporting lines that surface the occasional case.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate links each corruption pattern to a control frequency and says why. A strong answer argues that systemic risk demands universal checks while sporadic risk can be met by sampling.
questions.hint: Ask how often each pattern would trigger a check.

questions.learningObjective: Identify grand corruption from the scale of a single diverted decision
questions.stem: An engineer's brief notes that a single pipeline contract absorbed 40 per cent of the regional works budget in one year.

options.text: The contract is an example of petty corruption because it involved one official signing one decision

options.text: The contract is an example of sporadic corruption because it happened in one region only
options.misconception: confuses regional spread with a sporadic pattern

options.text: The contract is an example of grand corruption because a huge sum was diverted through one decision

questions.explanation: Grand corruption is identified by the scale of the value and the level of the decision involved, not by how many officials took part. One decision that diverts 40 per cent of a budget is grand on any schedule.
questions.hint: Ask about the size of the sum and the level of the decision.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a structural concentration of awards and links as a capture pattern

stimulus.body: Three firms won 71 per cent of the contracts in the sector over two years, and each of the three has a former officer on the sector's technical committee, which sets the scoring rules. The committee's own report notes that it has not considered whether this concentration might affect its judgments. Separately, an unrelated audit found the committee's scoring sheets followed the published criteria in every file it checked.

questions.stem: The engineer's brief quotes a transparency review; the relevant passage is reproduced below.

options.text: The concentration shows capture because no firm won more than a quarter of the contracts
options.misconception: reads a concentration of share as no concentration at all

options.text: The audit finding proves capture because disciplined scoring is a classic sign of a captured body
options.misconception: treats procedural tidiness as evidence of capture

options.text: The concentration and officer links fit a capture pattern, while the audit only shows scoring was followed

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the uses and limits of a published corruption index
questions.stem: A ministry asks the engineer to explain, in plain terms for a design brief, what a published corruption index can and cannot tell a reader about a district.

answer.exemplar: A corruption index is a composite score, usually built from expert and public perception, that ranks or classifies countries or sectors by how corrupt they appear to be. It is useful for tracking broad movement over time and comparing places on one scale. It cannot tell the reader how many bribes were paid, who took them, which service stage was affected, or what happened in any particular district, because it aggregates judgement rather than recording events.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate states what the index aggregates and refuses to over-read it as an event count. A strong answer separates comparative uses from local detail it cannot supply.
questions.hint: Say what the index aggregates and what it omits.

The perception score must be wrong, since no district can stay unchanged for three full years
options.misconception: treats a flat series as proof of measurement failure

options.text: The fall in complaints must be wrong, because perception did not move to confirm it
options.misconception: requires one series to confirm the other

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify that a corruption index aggregates perception rather than recording events

stimulus.body: The index is produced twice a year. It begins with expert assessments of how corrupt each country's public administration appears, and with survey responses from people who deal with public officials. These two sets of judgements are converted to scores, scaled and combined into a single number for each country. The note records that no individual bribe, payment or official is identified anywhere in the process, and that the same respondents are asked the same questions each round so results remain comparable.

questions.stem: The engineer's brief cites a description of a national index; the relevant passage is reproduced below.

options.text: The index aggregates perception into one comparable score and does not record identifiable bribery events
The index records bribery events in each country because the survey responses describe them directly
options.misconception: assumes survey answers become event records

options.text: The index cannot compare countries because the responses come from different kinds of respondent
options.misconception: assumes mixed respondent types defeat comparability

options.text: The index is unusable because asking the same questions each round prevents any change being detected
options.misconception: confuses standardisation with the absence of change

questions.explanation: The method note describes aggregated judgement, not enumerated events. Standardised questions make rounds comparable, so the index tracks shifts in perceived corruption rather than particular payments.
questions.hint: Ask whether any individual event is recorded.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why capture is harder to remove than isolated bribery
questions.stem: A reform team asks the engineer to explain, for a design brief, what state capture looks like in a licensing system and why it is harder to remove than isolated bribery.

answer.exemplar: Capture is not a single bribe but a standing arrangement in which the people who make a decision on behalf of the public are shaped by the interests of the parties they decide about, and gradually make those interests their own. In a licensing system it appears as criteria drifting towards a connected firm's requirements, licences clustering among a small group, and rules that look formal but are written around one set of applicants. Removing it is harder than removing isolated bribery because it sits in who advises, who scores and who benefits, so those posts must be opened up, not just the payments cleaned up.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate defines capture as a structural arrangement rather than a series of payments and connects that to the reform required. A strong answer locates the interests in rules and roles.
questions.hint: Show where the informal interest sits in the system.

options.misconception: trusts direct observation as a complete measure

questions.hint: Ask what each tool counts or judges.

options.misconception: assumes disclosure alone removes influence

questions.learningObjective: Interpret reported experience rising while perceived stability holds

options.misconception: dismisses a series for being short rather than inconsistent

options.text: Reported incidence can rise while perceived stability holds, because the two measures sample different things

options.misconception: assumes bad faith without any evidence of it

options.text: Resident reports count too many minor payments to show the real level of corruption in the district
options.misconception: dismisses small events without comparing the two series

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why delegation creates a conflict between private gain and the public objective
questions.stem: A senior administrator asks the engineer to explain, for the design brief, why a principal-agent problem arises when a public body delegates a service to a private operator.

answer.exemplar: Delegation separates the party whose objectives matter from the party that carries out the work, and the operator is paid in a way that need not reward what the public body wants. If payment depends on volume, cases handled or work completed, the operator's income can rise while service quality, fairness or coverage for residents falls. Because the public body cannot always observe effort and outcome directly, the operator's private calculation pulls the service away from the public objective. The response is to design payment and information so that the operator's own gain comes from what the public body wants.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate links delegation to a payment rule rewarding the wrong outcome rather than listing examples. A strong answer explains why private gain conflicts with the public objective.
questions.hint: Connect the payment rule to the operator's own gain.

options.misconception: explains drift by ease of supervision

options.text: The agency has drifted because promotion and budget now reward whatever the newest priority is

questions.hint: Ask what the agency now gains by shifting its work.

questions.learningObjective: Identify dependence created by who drafts the rules an administrative body applies

stimulus.body: The audit found that the committee which drafts the specification for road contracts meets in the offices of an association whose membership is made up of the main contractors in the sector. options.text: The audit proves capture, because the specification is written in an association office

The audit shows the sector is captured, because no firm bid twice in the same quarter

questions.explanation: Capture can operate through rule setting rather than individual decisions. Here the interested party shapes the specification the committee applies, so outcomes follow their interests even when every criterion is met.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish drift from a simple failure to perform
questions.stem: A council asks the engineer to explain, in a short paragraph for the brief, how agency drift differs from a straightforward failure to perform.

answer.exemplar: A failure to perform is a shortfall against a target the agency still accepts: the work is wanted, the standard is known and the problem is capacity, funding or competence. Drift is different because the target itself has lost force. The agency's attention has moved to other work that its professional rewards, budget rules or reporting lines make more attractive, so it still claims to serve the original purpose while spending its effort elsewhere. That is why a failure can be fixed with more resources and a better plan, while drift needs the rewards around the agency to be reset before the original mandate regains priority.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate separates a shortfall in execution from a shift in what the agency tries to do. A strong answer points to differing remedies: failure invites resources, drift invites incentives.
questions.hint: Ask whether the agency still accepts its target.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an unwritten standing rule from a burst of coincidental payments

stimulus.body: We followed 400 administrative decisions at one permitting office over two years. Two hundred and seventy-two of the decisions involved a payment of a fixed sum to the clerk, regardless of the size or value of the request, and the office continued to operate while staff accepted the practice openly. In a second office with comparable staffing, we found 19 such payments, all occurring in a single fortnight before a supervisor was transferred. The fixed-sum rule at the first office did not appear in any written instruction.

questions.stem: The engineer attaches a research summary to the brief; the summary is reproduced below.

options.text: The first office shows sporadic corruption, since no payment was written into an instruction
options.misconception: requires a written rule for a pattern to be systemic

options.text: The second office shows systemic corruption, because payments there were larger on average
options.misconception: reads size of payments as a measure of the pattern

options.text: Both offices show the same pattern, because both produced payments to the office clerk
options.misconception: groups cases by actor rather than by pattern

options.text: The first office fits a systemic pattern and the second a sporadic one, given how payments are distributed

questions.explanation: Systemic corruption appears as a rule applied across cases, written or not. The fixed sum on 272 of 400 decisions is such a rule; 19 payments tied to one fortnight and a staff change are scattered.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why petty corruption resists detection better than grand corruption
questions.stem: A journalist asks the engineer to explain, for a brief on municipal contracting, why petty corruption is often harder to detect than grand corruption.

answer.exemplar: Grand corruption is concealed through complexity: large contracts are negotiated over many months, priced in ways that are hard to compare, and settled through layers of subcontracting, so the diversion leaves few obvious traces and needs expert tracing to see. Petty corruption is concealed through volume and smallness: each payment is trivial, is taken at a routine counter, and is denied by both parties, so nothing looks wrong and no single case attracts attention. Because it repeats, the total cost of petty corruption can be large, and the detection method that works for one case will not work for a pattern.

questions.explanation: The item tests whether the candidate explains why the two kinds hide differently rather than ranking them by size. A strong answer links concealment to scale, repetition and audit cost.
questions.hint: Ask how each kind is hidden from ordinary review.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Show how paying per inspection can diverge from the residents' interest in safety
questions.stem: An engineer is told the agency that inspects lifts is paid per inspection completed, while residents are the ones who ride them.

options.text: The agency's income rises with more inspections whether or not residents are better served, so interests diverge
No problem arises, because every completed inspection makes the lifts safer for the residents
options.misconception: assumes activity volume equals service quality

options.text: The problem is that residents do not pay the agency directly for the inspections
options.misconception: requires the principal to pay the agent directly

options.text: The problem is that residents have no way of complaining about the number of inspections
options.misconception: mistakes a complaint channel for the incentive problem

questions.explanation: Agency pay rises with the number of inspections, not with lift condition, so more inspections can mean more income and no better service. Residents hold the interest the rule ignores.
questions.hint: Ask what the payment rule rewards.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise drift in budget allocations where the mandate's share shrinks over time
questions.stem: A brief table shows an agency's stated purpose alongside where its budget actually went across three years.

options.text: Because the stated purpose never changed, the agency cannot have drifted from its mandate
options.misconception: assumes a fixed charter prevents drift

options.text: The shrinking share going to the mandate, while other lines grow, is what drift looks like in budgets
Budget shares are not evidence of drift, because drift is a matter of intent rather than allocation
options.misconception: treats drift as needing deliberate intent

options.text: The agency has drifted, because its published purpose was written in unusually broad language
options.misconception: explains drift by broad drafting of the purpose

questions.explanation: Drift shows in allocation before it shows in argument. If the share of the budget attached to the mandate falls year after year while other lines grow, the agency is pulled towards rewarded work.
questions.hint: Ask where the money went over time.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the principal among parties who carry risk, hold power and are served
questions.stem: A council's design brief for a market redevelopment names the traders who will trade there, the developers who will build it, and the officers who will approve the plans.

options.text: The developers are the principal, since they carry the construction risk that the scheme creates
options.misconception: equates bearing risk with the principal role

options.text: The officers are the principal, since they hold the approval power over the development
options.misconception: equates decision power with the principal role

options.text: The traders are the principal, since the scheme exists to serve the market they will trade in
The council is the principal, since the council is the body that delegated the redevelopment
options.misconception: confuses the delegating body with the principal for a delegated contract

questions.explanation: The principal role follows the objectives the delegated work serves. The redevelopment is authorised to provide trading space, while developers carry risk and officers hold approval power, neither one the principal.
questions.hint: Ask who the scheme was created to serve.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a composite corruption score from three equally weighted components
questions.stem: A composite corruption risk score for the engineer's region averages three equally weighted components scoring 62, 48 and 55. What is the composite score?
questions.explanation: The three components sum to 165, and equal weighting divides that by three, which gives 55. Such a composite condenses several judgements into one comparable figure, which hides which component drove it.
questions.hint: Average the three equally weighted component scores.
